text:
Jacek Karpiński (1927–2010) was a Polish computer engineer renowned for designing some of the country's most significant computing hardware during the Communist era. His career began with the construction of the **AAH** (Analytical Analyzer of Harmonics) in 1957, a vacuum-tube computer used to improve weather forecasts, followed by his breakthrough achievement, **AKAT-1** in 1959. AKAT-1 was the world's first transistor-based differential equations analyzer, featuring an innovative aesthetic design and a panel created by leading Polish artists.
Karpiński's most ambitious project was the **KAR-65** , a scientific computer built in 1968 to process data from CERN's bubble chambers. Operating at 100,000 operations per second, it was the fastest Polish computer of its time and utilized a custom asynchronous architecture and floating-point representation. His final major engineering feat was the **K-202** , a highly innovative minicomputer designed in 1973 that used Intel 4004 chips, memory segmentation, and floating-point math. Although only 30 units were produced due to political interference and lack of industrial backing, the K-202 was technologically superior to contemporary competitors like the PDP-11. After facing censorship and controversy regarding his past as a secret intelligence informant, Karpiński later worked in Switzerland and advised Polish economists, passing away in 2010.
